i ntroduction
Clustering techniques fall into two major categories, hierarchical techniques and optimiza-
tion or partitioned techniques.
h ierarchical t echniques
Hierarchical clustering can be broken down into two major categories agglomerative methods
and divisive methods. A procedure for forming agglomerative hierarchical groups of mutu-
ally exclusive subsets based on the premise that the greatest amount of information, as indi-
cated by the objective function, is available when a set of n members is ungrouped. The first
step is to select and combine the two subsets out of the n possible subsets which would pro-
duce the least impairment of the optimum value of the objective function, while reducing
the number of subsets to n − 1. These n − 1 subsets are then examined to identify which two
subsets should be merged in order to obtain the optimum value of the objective function for
n − 2 subsets. This procedure is repeated until the original n members are in a single set or
group. Since the number of subsets is reduced by one at each step (n, n − 1, ... , 1), the pro-
cess is referred to as hierarchical grouping. The grouping which occurs at each step usually
results in some quantifiable loss. The functional relation used to obtain a value-reflecting
number is called the objective function. In general, an objective function may be any func-
tional relationship that an investigator selects to reflect the relative desirability of groupings.
The objective function represents loss of information and is reflected by the error sum of
squares, (known as Ward’s Method). Other examples of objective functions can include:
1. the grand sum of the squared deviations about the means of all measured charac-
teristics, people are clustered to maximize their similarity with respect to measured
characteristics,
2. the expected cross-training time in the clustering of jobs to minimize cross-training
time when personnel are reassigned according to established policies,
3. the amount of job time incorrectly described to minimize errors. When clustering job
descriptions in describing a large number of jobs with a small number of descriptions, and
4. the loss of predictive efficiency when clustering regression equations to minimize
the loss of predicted efficiency resulting from reductions in the number of regression
equations judgmental analysis (JAN).
An important concept to remember in defining the hierarchical grouping mentioned above is
that once two entities are merged, they are joined permanently and become a building block
for later merges. This is one of the key differences between the hierarchical techniques and
the optimal techniques to be discussed in the next section. Another difference between the

two methods is how they arrive at the number of groups. If researchers are not interested in
the entire hierarchical tree structure, they must decide at what point the best clustering has
been reached. There are many different techniques available to help the user make a selection.
Some of the more common hierarchical techniques are the nearest neighbor (single linkage)
method, the farthest neighbor (complete linkage) method, centroid method, and Ward’s method
560 n n n r e S earch Metho DS for I N for M at I o N Sy S te MS n ch apter 42
(mentioned earlier in the chapter). The basic technique for these methods is similar. However,
there are two factors that differentiate between the methods. The first factor is whether the
technique can be used with similarity measures, distance measures, or both. The second factor
is how these measures are defined, or, in Ward’s terminology, the objective function.
In divisive clustering the initial starting point is with all entities in one group. The first step is
to split the group into two subsets. Subsequent steps consist of subdividing the subsets until
each entity is a separate group. There are two classes of methods for deciding how to split
the groups. With the monothetic methods, the data points are based on binary variables and
the object is to split the data set on one of these variables so as to minimize the value of some
appropriate measure of similarity between the two groups. The splitting process, based on
other variables, continues until some criterion is reached. Examples of monothetic techniques
include association analysis and the automatic interaction detector method. The polythetic
methods are based on the values taken by all of the variables. The divisive techniques have not
gained the same popularity as the agglomerative techniques and their use is minimal.
Optimization t echniques
The basic method used by the optimization techniques is to obtain an initial partition of the
data units and then alter the cluster membership to get a better partition, i.e., until a local
optimum is found. The various methods differ as to how they arrive at an initial partition and
how they define “better” (i.e., the objective function). The techniques in this section differ
from the hierarchical techniques in two ways. First, members are allowed to change cluster
membership. So, a data point poorly classified in an early cycle can be re-classified in a later
step. Second, the number of clusters must be specified in advance. If the structure of the
data is known a priori, this is not a problem. Otherwise, two possible suggestions are to:
1. try a number of different partitions, or
2. use a hierarchical technique first to help decide upon the number of clusters.

where T is the total dispersion matrix and W and B are the matrices of within-cluster and

In the k-means approach, once the initial partitions have been established, the cluster cen-
troid can be updated after each addition to the cluster (MacQueen’s method), or only after
all the points have been allocated (Forgy method and Jancey method).
The basic algorithm for MacQueen’s method is as follows:
1. Begin with an initial partition of the data units into clusters (any of the methods men-
tioned earlier will work).
2. Take each data unit in sequence and compute the distances to all cluster centroids; if
the nearest centroid is not that of the data unit’s parent cluster, then reassign the data
unit and update the centroids of the losing and gaining clusters.
3. Repeat step 2 until convergence is achieved; that is, continue until a full cycle
through the data set fails to cause any changes in cluster membership.
The basic algorithm for Forgy’s method is to:
1. Begin with any desired initial configuration. Go to step 2 if beginning with a set of
seed points; go to step 3 if beginning with a partition of the data units.
2. Allocate each data unit to the cluster with the nearest seed point. The seed points
remain fixed for a full cycle through the entire data set.
3. Compute new seed points as the centroids of the clusters of data units.
4. Alternate steps 2 and 3 until the process converges; that is, continue until no data
units change their cluster membership at step 2.
At this point a local optimum has been achieved. Unfortunately, there is no way to know
whether this is also the global optimum. The solution can either be accepted, or a new initial
partition can be obtained and the clusters can be re-analyzed.

43.1 i ntroduction
This chapter provides an overview of statistical software. Sketches of answers are provided
for responding to: What considerations are important in the design of a statistical software
package? What design constructs are possible? How can packages be compared? How can a
researcher select the package which best suits their needs?
In many, if not most situations, the researcher will not be able to choose from the entire array
of all available packages, but will have to select from a more limited list of the packages avail-
able. The questions above remain important, however, for choosing wisely from this limited
list and for using the selected package efficiency and effectively.
43.2 d esign c onstructs
Current statistical software packages designs are dependent upon what type of interface
is implemented. Several packages interface with relational database systems such as
ORACLE. Other packages interface with mathematical software. For instance MATLAB
is one which not only offers statistical capabilities but optimization and symbolic
manipulation. Some packages utilize visualization interfaces, which is a very useful fea-
ture for exploratory data analysis. User interfaces come in many sizes and shapes as they
have evolved from command line to graphical user interfaces to hybrid drag and drop
system interfaces.
An applications software package, in statistics or in any other area, may take one of these
four forms:
1. A set of independent programs.
2. A set of subroutines to be called by a user-generated program.
3. A single, multipurpose program.
4. An applications compiler.
The design of a package must take into account a number of considerations, including:
1. The intended application of the package (primarily the behavioral sciences, some
other area, or a number of fields).
2. The background of users (undergraduates or professional statisticians).
3. The level of experience of the users (familiarity with computers and programming).
4. The hardware the package will run on.
We now consider the four major design constructs in more detail.

43.2.1 s ets of programs
In a package of this kind, each program is complete in itself, and each performs just one statis-
tical operation on the data file: computing descriptive statistics, for example, or performing a
t-test. Each program will use the same input formatting, style of documentation, and coding
language, and some effort will also be made to standardize the output formats. The advan-
tages of such a package are these: the programs can be easily used by a nonprogrammer, and

36907.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36907.heading: 43.7 Statistical c omputing e xercises
36907.content:
they generally offer some flexibility of input format. In many cases, however, the user will
want to perform many analyses on a particular data file, or the same analysis on several files.
A package of individual programs is clumsy and time consuming in such situations.
43.2.2 s ets of subroutines
When the package consists of a set of subroutines, the user must write a main program to
read in the data file and call the subroutines to perform statistical analyses. This main pro-
gram will be written in a high-level language, while the subroutines will be entirely input-
free. There are several advantages to such a package
1. Statistical processing can be tailored to each job.
2. Repetitive runs of several programs can be done easily.
3. Routines not in the package can be supplied by the user.
On the other hand, a set of subroutines can be used only by someone familiar with program-
ming in the language of the subroutines; many statistical users will not have such training.
Packages of this type generally have less documentation provided than might be required by
the general user. Therefore, a high level of sophistication in computing may be required to
obtain statistical results.

43.2.3 Large, multiple-use programs
Many packages today are single, large programs and can be divided into two subcatego-
ries. In the first, the entire program, which can perform a variety of statistical and pro-
cessing tasks, is maintained in the computer’s memory. Such packages tend to occupy vast
amounts of storage, and they can require large amounts of time for I/O. They are, how-
ever, easily used by the nonprogrammer. In the second, the first section of code loaded
into main memory produces a menu of available operations, then generates calls to the
parts of the program which perform tasks the user requests, either in a specified code
or in some language prose series of statements. Only those parts of the program related
to the current tasks are maintained in memory, which can then be used more efficiently.
Such systems are well-adapted to interactive use, and some also provide tutorial sessions
in the use of the package.
43.2.4 a pplication compilers
Packages of this type are, in fact, programming languages in which statistical tasks, or large
steps in statistical tasks, are initiated by single statements in the language. They are useful to
the researcher who wants to perform a nonstandard analysis quickly, but they again require

that the user be a competent programmer. Implementation of a statistical applications
compiler can be accomplished with a functional paradigm programming language.
43.3 p roblem a reas
Many, if not most statistical packages, now in wide use were written by programmers
rather than statisticians. Today many package systems are constructed in modules
and adapted to current technology but with minimal documentation. These and other
conditions have led to the following problem areas in the design and use of statistical
packages:
1. Statistical packages are often misunderstood, inefficiently used, even misused.
The ease with which some packages can be used may encourage the unwary to apply the
analyses in the package to situations and data inconsistent with the techniques available. For
example, assume that a group of values has come from a normally distributed population
when this has not been established. Documentation should show not only how to cause the
analyses to be performed but also the situations to which the analyses are applicable, the
assumptions on which the techniques are based, and the conclusions that can be drawn. This
information should be available not only in the written documentation of the package but
also in online tutorial help sessions.
2. Overly stringent requirements of system hardware or software.
Some packages are written for specific architectural platforms, and can be used only with
difficulty, if at all, on any other platform. Some require specialized devices, a plotter, for

example, that may not be available.
3. Lack of transportability.
It should be possible to execute a package on a wide variety of architectures, par-
ticularly since hardware/software changes at computer facilities occur with surprising
frequency. Acquisition of a new machine should not render all purchased software
unusable. Import/export facilities are extremely important components needed in cur-
rent applications. For instance, Excel has been widely used for entry and management
of data.
4. Inflexible and complicated user interfaces.
In some earlier packages, the statements used to control the operation of the package seemed
almost intentionally obscure, with stringent requirements for the placement of instructions
on each line and instructions which, at first glance, seem arbitrary sequences of characters.
Graphical user interfaces greatly enhance the usability of a package and should be easily
accessible to those who use it. In particular, English-like words should be used, and their
placement on the lines should not be overly critical.

6. Sophistication of programming language design.
The language in which the package is written is clearly relevant to its performance.
There are many issues in programming language design which relate to package perfor-
mance, for which we will provide one example. Subroutines may be classified as open or
closed. A closed subroutine (or subprocedure, or subprogram) is compiled and stored in
the computer’s memory separately from the main program that calls it. A call statement
in the main program causes a jump in the flow of execution into the subroutine and at
the completion of the subroutine, execution returns to the point in the main program
immediately after the call. Such a linking mechanism need not reside in memory simul-
taneously with its main program except when the subroutine is executed. The code of an
open subroutine, in contrast, is a part of the code of the main program, the subroutine
is compiled and resides in memory with its main program. Many modern computers

closed subroutines. If many users are engaging the computer, there may be insufficient
memory remaining to bring in a closed subroutine. Thus, that program will wait until
other executions are completed and sufficient space in memory is freed to bring in the
subroutine.
7. Lack of modularity.
Many early packages are composed of large blocks of code not broken down into modular
sections. Such code is difficult to maintain or modify, and often lacks transportability because
machine-dependent statements are hard to locate. Object oriented paradigm programming
languages alleviate this problem.

It is obvious that the single most desirable characteristic of any package of programs is ease

operation in these areas can be more of an impediment than an aid. Other useful character-

approximation of the situation represented by the data. Graphical displays are
desirable here.
2. An English-like command structure.
3. Intelligible error messages during execution to avoid dependence on the documentation.
4. Results in English sentences whenever possible, rather than just tables of values.
5. The ability to generate new values based on existing values.
6. The inclusion of a end-user friendly graphical user interface.
7. Hardcopy documentation and online help sessions/tutorials showing examples of data
files, runs using the package, and interpretation of results.
8. The ability to manipulate data files.
This last characteristic deserves further comment. In addition to sorting of files, the attach-
ment labels to variables, and the selection of particular cases, it is also often useful to invert
a file, that is, to rearrange the records in a new order based on the values of a particular
variable.

44.1 i ntroduction
A college major in computer science would classify computational complexity as a theoretical
or foundational topic. The same student would also classify data structures or design of algo-
rithms as applied computer science studies. What is the difference between theoretical and
applied studies? The student’s perception probably leads them in this direction based upon
operationally defining applied areas of study as those studies being real-world-solutions to
real-world-problems. At the same time, the student probably perceives areas of study that
expand knowledge in the field as theoretical.
However, appearances can be deceptive. Many of the topics covered in computational
complexity classes evolved from real-world problems, such as the need for determining if a
problem is solvable with a specific architecture. On the other hand, attempting to solve real-
world-problems can help one to discover new knowledge and is, therefore, defined as usually
theoretical. There appears to be a non-empty intersection between theoretical and applied
domains. Possibly it is better to think of application as a catalyst for expanding knowledge in
the field and theoretical studies as preparation for application.
44 .2 s ample s tudy
The study discussed here is a cognitive-map-based approach to the coordination of distrib-
uted cooperative agents available online at http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/.
Ternary logic is employed, through the use of negative-positive-neural logic (NPN), in this
study to allow for response to stimuli by representative states of “agreement, disagreement,
or maybe.” Using NPN components, the researchers have has constructed a pooled cognitive
map that is derived from a network of cognitive maps. Each node in the network represents
either an Artificial Intelligent (AI) agent’s or a human agent’s cognitive map; it represents the
agent’s positive to negative reactions to stimuli. The network is implemented in the LISP and
C programming languages.
A typical application for this system consists of gathering a group of both AI and human experts
on a domain area to consider a specific problem. The system, called D-POOL, commences
with several of the local nodes, broadcasting the problem statement throughout the network.
Next a determination of the identity of valid experts as well as pooling the cognitive maps, is
derived from their assigned groups. Finally, all the originally chosen local nodes, or experts,
have their cognitive map stored. When the problem of interest is presented to each expert

The basic need for this hypothesis test includes the following issues:

We are left with asking what criteria could be used to determine whether a theory is an
adequate one. A number of such criteria can be found in the literature. However, it must be
recognized that their application is a matter of rational analysis and can give only a general
indication of theoretical adequacy. This theory from the field of study in distributed artificial

c riteria for adequacy testing theory
n Testability — A theory should lead to deductions that can be credited or discredited
by empirical test.
n Consistency — A theory should be free from internal contradiction or be logically
consistent.
n Scope — A theory should account for a relatively wide range of data.
n Predictive power — A theory should provide a basis for successful prediction.
n Fruitfulness — A theory should generate a variety of new hypotheses.
n Parsimony — Other things being equal, a simpler theory is preferable to a more
complicated one.
Of these, predictive power is perhaps the acid test of a theory. Two points should be made,
however. The first is that the theory selected for use here is seen as one way of approach-

The use of product design and development processes across multiple companies is referred
to as Collaborative Product Development (CPD). Usually this calls for transparent integra-
tion across heterogeneous computer center architecture and system/application system plat-
forms. CPD can improve product launch success and, therefore, have an impact on reducing
cost and speeding up time to market. Mandatory benefits of a CPD should include sharing
specifications, test results, design changes, and the use of online prototyping, and customer
feedback processing. Shared and integrated information may realize reduced development
costs and time due to tightly integrating and streamlining communication channels.
Every product development process should ask:
1. What are the needs of the customer?
2. How large of a potential market is there for the product?
3. What is the perceived product modification cycle and projected half-life for the product?
Then using the SCM data flows, the following chain of events can be conducted: planning
for design, the actual manufacturing process for the product, and for producing the product.
Rather than having each of the functional and business components corporately organized
as a disconnected network of independent islands of knowledge, CPDs offer an architectural
supportive of product design and development, as well as new product development. The
end result of the CPDs is the development, processing, and customer delivery that gets the
product to the customer cheaply, timely, and with high quality and, simultaneously, main-

Whether a research study is labeled as applied or theoretical is immaterial. What is impor-

Study Discovery of Functional and Approximate Functional Dependencies in Relational
Databases available at http://www.emis.de/journals/HOA/JAMDS/7/149.pdf. This study
develops the foundation for a simple, yet efficient method for uncovering functional and
approximate functional dependencies in relational databases.

The technique is based upon
the mathematical theory of partitions done over a relation’s row identifiers. Using a level-

putations conducted on integers. Therefore, the required operations on partitions are both
simple and fast. Additionally, the row identifiers provide the added advantage of nominally
identifying the exceptions to approximate functional dependencies, which can be used effec-

45.3 a xiomatic d evelopment as a r esearch m ethod
Assume that you are a new employee for a globally sized company and put in charge of
designing the corporate database. How will you convince the management and stakeholders

for all practical matters, the database appears to us as infinitely large. Thanks to the axiom-

semantics can be rigorously and ruthlessly specified.

1. A relation is a uniquely named two dimensional table.
2. An attribute is a uniquely named, within the definition of the relation, column of the

8. Each attribute of a relation is a domain; that is a particular data type.
9. If an assigned value to an attribute X forces another attribute Y to have a specific
value, then X functionally determines Y and is denoted as X → Y. X → Y is called a
functional dependency.
10. A set of two or more attributes is a key for a relation R if:
a. those attributes functionally determine all other attributes of the relation, and
b. no proper subset of the set of attributes functionally determines all other attri-
butes of R, this minimal set of attributes is called a primary key.

45.8 t he a xiomatic m ethod as a t ool for r esearch
The major value of the axiomatic method is its use as a tool for opening up vast new domains
for investigation. Use of the axiomatic method in teaching affords the student a chance to
experience the thrill of creating concepts and to glimpse the inherent beauty of the field
under study. The axiomatic method not only encourages researchers to develop their own
creative powers, but sometimes leads to the invention of new methods not previously con-
ceived. A great merit of the axiomatic approach, as illustrated in both the sample study article
and the discussion in previous sections, is that it admits the possibility of a mixture of deduc-
tive and empirical thinking. Axiomatic development is simply the application of the scientific
method to problems classically recognized as purely theoretical.

Solving a research problem is like solving a detective mystery. The task requires planning and
the careful collection of facts. With a little planning, your research experience can be posi-

Simulation typically is nothing more or less than the technique of performing sampling
experiments on the model of the system. The experiments are done on the model rather than
on the real system itself only because the latter would be too inconvenient, expensive, and
time consuming. Otherwise, simulated experiments should be viewed as virtually indistin-
guishable from ordinary statistical experiments, so that they also should be based upon sound
statistical theory. Simulated experiments usually are executed on a computer because of the
vast amount of data being generated and processed rather than because of any inherent rela-
tionship between the experiment and the computer.

46.1 Introduction
The methodology of simulation, initially used by operations research, was created by John
von Neumann and Stanislaw Ulam in the late 1940s. Since the advent of digital computing,
simulation has been used for countless business applications. Essentially, simulation is the
use of a system model that has the desired characteristics of reality in order to reproduce
the essence of the actual operations. The Monte Carlo method is simulation by sampling
techniques. It involves determining the probability distribution of the variable under con-
sideration and then sampling from this distribution by means of random numbers to obtain
data. In effect, a set of random numbers is used to generate a set of values that have the same
distributional characteristics as the actual experience it is desired to simulate. In this chapter,
we will study Monte Carlo simulation with actual business applications.

Chapter 46 presented a brief overview of the Monte Carlo Method. This technique is a
computational technique applied to static models. Static models provide for the relationship
between the system attributes when the system is in equilibrium. If a point of equilibrium
is changed by altering any of the attribute values, then the model enables the new values for
all the attributes to be derived. However, the model does not show ‘how’ the attribute values
were modified.
Dynamic models follow the changes over time that result from the system attributes. In
this chapter, an algorithm for a discrete event simulation is presented through applying the
dynamic model which maintains a current events chain. A polling and reassignment of attri-
bute values take place each time an event experiences a change of state.

47.3 d iscrete e vent s imulation
The previous examples of simulation we discussed did not involve time as an element of the
simulation. Such simulations are referred to as static. However, many systems experience
changes in state over time. For example, inventory and queuing systems have the state vari-
ables change only at a discrete set of points in time and are called discrete event simulations.
But consider the water behind a dam. Clearly evaporation and heavy rains make the state
variable. The water level experiences changes in state continuously over time. Systems like
this are referred to as continuous simulations.
Consider simulating a network system. For this type of study, the researcher must:
n Identify the system, which is a collection of entities that interact over time to
accomplish the goals of the study.
n Construct a model, or an abstract representation of the system that describes a
system in terms of state, entities and related attributes, sets, events, activities, and
delays.
c The system state is a collection of variables that contain all of the information to
describe the system at any time.
c A set is simply a collection of associated states.
c An event is an occurrence that changes the state of a system.
c A known time interval, such as for servicing an entity, is an activity.
c A time interval of unknown length until an activity is actually completed, such as a
wait time in a queue, is referred to as a delay.
When setting up a discrete event simulation, one must operationally define the system state,

48.1 i ntroduction
This chapter is a short descriptive tour through a hypothetical research study. The purpose
of the vignette is to point out tips of advice on practical issues the researcher should prac-
tice while conducting research. The vignette presented is resolved through experimentation.
Experimentation has broad applications in the computing field.
48.2 t he v ignette s etting
A commercial software design and development firm is concerned about how to ensure
product quality efficiently to their customer base. As a result the corporate management
board has placed several of the software design and development personnel on a team to
identify and determine which aspects of attributes prompt meeting delivery deadlines and
produce quality software in their industry. Clearly, the answer can be derived from several
diverse viewpoints and motives.
Any good software project manager would take attribute measurements of the process and
product in order to forecast delivery time and the expected budget. Customers would per-
form a feature analysis of the product with respect to their requirements and make an assess-
ment of adequate quality. Corporate management would need to determine if upgrades
were needed for meeting customer satisfaction.
Is this project noteworthy?
The effectiveness of research demands depend greatly on the proper selection of projects. In
the corporate world top level management should play a part in the project selection process
due to the fact that the benefits from research projects cross functional and business func-
tion boundaries. Therefore, since this vignette is hypothetical, this project has been deter-
mined to be noteworthy and already passed the first hurdle in becoming a research study.
Select Research Projects Carefully.
48.3 p reliminary r esearch s tudy s tatement
Anyone that has participated in a software development project, whether as a student or a
professional, knows that screening and reporting relevant data on pertinent attributes and
development processes of the software relate to the answer. The study team’s past experi-
ences would make them keenly aware that there must be an assessment of participant’s
progress in any project as well as assessment of the product’s quality. Most of the study team
would consider the variety of measurement techniques used by a software engineer.
Integrate your experiences and educational background into the research study.

48.4 b ackground r eview
A thorough background review should be immediately initiated: a literature search, both
an internet and web search, commercial software development shop visitations, interview/
questionnaire surveys of successful/experienced software development project personnel,
and any other creative ideas of searching for information. Identification of academic and
professional societies pertinent to the study would be necessary. Also identification of key
individuals or experts within the field of the study would be required.
The participants in the background study need answers for:
What are the attributes of concern?
What is the impact of the attributes of concern on software development?
Who are some of the nationally known experts in the domain of software development mea-
surement?
Which professional / academic societies are pertinent to the study?
Are there any available RFPs applicable to the study?
Each team member should list at least 6 researchable questions for future research projects
in the study domain.

37076.content:
48.5 Formulating a p roject that can be r esolved
For the sake of illustration, let’s assume that the study team has settled on using software
product metrics and software development process metrics. The team has reached agree-
ment that two major merits for product metrics are that product quality is measureable and
product attribute characteristics are quantifiable.
Goodness criteria for the product is a very controllable and well-defined domain, especially
in software engineering. However, the process metrics area is overwhelming and as a result,
the research team would be aware that it is absolutely necessary to complete both a Joint
Application Development (JAD) session and pilot testing of candidate attributes and poten-
tial analysis models.
JAD is a technique for including users in the development of a new system. The JAD sessions
are generally conducted in specially configured rooms, with the final outcome being general
agreement between users and system professionals as to general information requirements
of the business. JAD sessions are extremely appropriate during system planning and system
analysis phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC). This would be a perfect
technique to use in the study since the members of the study team would be so familiar with
it. JAD sessions would enable the study team, corporate management, customer representa-
tives, and other stakeholders to reach a consensus on attributes, metrics, and preliminary
analysis methods/models to be included in the study. A brief list of attributes would probably
626 n n n r e S earch Metho DS F or In F or M at I on Sy S te MS n ch apter 48
contain: productivity cost and resource requirements, effectiveness of quality, effectiveness
of development tools, and many others.
To complicate matters more is the fact that current software metrics are specific to a given
phase of the SDLC. For example the lines of code (LOC) can be used to measure the amount
of work done and predict size, but not before the project implementation phase begins. LOC
is commonly used to measure productivity. The study team could even consider using LOC
to measure quality. Detection of defaults is relevant only during the specification phase.
By this time the study team would realize that the project could get out of hand; downsizing
to make the study realistic as well as ensure that precise and accurate results be generated
might be required.
Always remember, be patient and strive for simplicity.
Be careful that the real problem is uncovered and solved rather than dealing with
symptoms of the actual problem.
Do not be a Robinson Crusoe, the world’s first system analyst. At one point of his island
story, he set out to build a dugout canoe. He located a fantastic tree in the exact center of the

37077.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37077.heading: 48.5 Formulating a p roject that can be r esolved
37077.sectionTitle: Formulating a p roject that can be r esolved
37077.content:
island. A fabulous canoe was manufactured by the obsessive Crusoe, but to no avail. It was
literally impossible to transport the final product to water. Another failed project! Research-
ers must realize that they do not need to construct an eight lane highway for someone’s
driveway at their private home.
48.6 a ttribute s creening
Guidelines and processes that will alleviate the attribute screening could require that:
1. Attribute Measurement is dependent upon the SDLC phases.
2. Scope and cost are among the most pertinent attributes, especially for measuring
aspects of product quality.
3. Should internal attributes, which are only directly measurable, or external attributes
be selected for the study?
At this juncture, it would be apparent that a pilot study should be implemented to finalize
the attribute list and investigate various models for the data analysis. The pilot study charge
should be to find out the answers to these questions for any available and accessible data.
Is the data meaningful?
What is the origin of the data?
Is the data complete?
Is the data understandable?
Is the data pertinent to the research?
Does the data meet the requirements for the proposed preliminary analysis methods?

37078.content:
chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 627
During these past components of the study, team members should not let themselves be
sidetracked! During screening, team members may have asked: ‘Is there a way to character-
ize metrics that may be directly related to quality, productivity, and technology?’ This would
be a great research project.
Several team members might have asked: ‘Should the firm invest in implementing efficient
fault tolerant software?’ Fault tolerance is a software/hardware technique where interven-
tion and prevention for system failures is employed. For example, defensive programming
based on redundancy can be used to cope with mistakes in the real environment. All software
faults result from design errors. Therefore, to implement fault tolerant computing for coping
with design faults, programs need to be tested repeatedly during run time and designed to
dynamically recover from errors. The fundamental method for implementing software fault
tolerance uses redundancy or alterations.
Consider the typical sort processing example. Assume that the software system allocates one
controller block, one recording block, and three sorting blocks to complete the sort. Each
request cycle begins with the controller block providing a copy of the original data file to the
first sorting block to sort. After this sorting block finishes sorting, a request is sent from the
controller block to the recording block to check whether the result is correct based upon
pre-established specifications. If this sorting block fails to produce the specified result, the
controller block will send another copy of the original data file to a different sorting block,
then begins execution. This process is repeated until the data is correctly sorted or no more
sorting blocks are available. In the latter case, the system fails.
Care must be taken; clearly, such activity by the study team indicates the team would have
become side-tracked.
Be patient!
Stay focused!
In the solution of a research study, new research projects are discovered.
Do not be discouraged, simply file these questions in your conceptual framework. These
research questions could become some of your future research studies. Congratulations
would be in order for the study team members!
Continuously build and enhance your conceptual domain.
Remember the three Ps.
Plan, prepare and then produce.
After completion of a well-defined pilot testing, attribute testing, and successful JAD ses-
sions the study team probably should have completed 90% of the overall study.

48.7 s tudy d esign
Consensus would have been reached obtained in the study by this time. Both product and pro-
cess metrics could have been chosen for inclusion in the study. Product metrics measure things

37079.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37079.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 627
37079.content:
like lines of code, whereas process metrics measure the efficiency of fault detection during
development. The project could have been directed to concentrate on scope and elapsed time.
Each type of metric measurement needing to be measured would be defined either using
internal or external attributes. Internal attributes are measured in terms of the entity itself.
External attributes represent a measure of the relationship to some external requirement
defined by the environment in which the entity is produced or used. For instances, software
code maintainability represents the ability of a specific product entity to adhere to accom-
modating changes in a reasonable manner. Another example is being able to modify the code
in one module without having to understand the code in another module.
It is likely that the study team would have decided that the study concentrate on attributes that
can be measured directly by examining the process, the product, and the resources applied.
Indirect measures can be obtained by establishing an empirical relationship between the
measure desired and other countable attributes of the entity. Counting man hours devoted
to a task is a direct measurement for the procedural design task. A module complexity attri-
bute can be determined indirectly through measuring other countable characteristics of the
software design logic such as the number of simple branch points in the algorithm. Then
complexity might simply be a function of the number of simple branches found in the code.
Process improvement through defect measurement and analyzes is facilitated by the nature
of the data collected. A modification of the Software Engineering Institute’s (SEI) Process
Maturity Model can be utilized. The usage of a nationally recognized standard lends validity
and reliability to the research study, especially internal validity and external validity.
Metrics can be chosen for each phase of the SDLC: specification, design, implementation
and integration, and maintenance. Time spent on specification development, size, effort, and
number of pages in the specification document could be used for the specification phase. The
number of modules as the size of the product, module cohesion and coupling as a measure of
the quality of the design, and fault statistics could be used for the design phase. Total num-
ber of test cases which result in a failure as well as other accurately kept fault statistics would
probably be utilized in the implementation phase. The metrics used for measurement in all
the other phases are pertinent to the metric measurements needed for the maintenance phase.
The discussion on screening for attributes implies that the research study would not have a
design but a collection of designs, indicated by the phases of the SDLC. In fact, the imple-

37080.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37080.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 627
37080.content:
mentation phase might help the study team in integrating these phases. Now, the team
should consider the screening process for selecting a good design.
What precisely is a research design? First it is a plan, structure, and strategy of the inves-
tigation to be conducted. Planning is actually the overall scheme or programmed activities
of the research. Such an program of activities includes everything that must be done by the
researcher from writing the hypothesis(es) to the analysis(es) of the data. The outline, scheme,
and modeling of the operation of the variables specify the structure of the design. Strategy is

37081.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37081.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 629
37081.content:
chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 629
composed of the methods for data gathering and analyzing the data. How research objectives
are reached and how to tackle the research problems is the purpose of the strategy.
What is the purpose of a research design? Primarily the purpose is to obtain answers to
the research questions. Second, the research is to control variance. The major emphasis in
research is to get answers to the questions while controlling for experimental, extraneous,
and error variances for the research studied.
A research design enables the researcher to answer research questions: with validity, objec-
tively, accurately, and with economic control. Design does not inform the researcher on what
to do, rather the design infers the direction of observation-making and analysis. Acceptable
designs must address:
How many observations should be made?
Which variables are active?
Which variables are assigned?
Researchers need to be able to manipulate the active variables and categorize the assigned
variables. Additionally, the design tells the researcher what type of statistical analysis, and/
or other methodologies, to use. More importantly, an adequate design will outline possible
conclusions to be derived from the statistical design.
Note that in the computing field, projects are not just limited to statistical analysis but can
involve measurement, simulation, and analytic modeling. Often the emphasis of the research
may be dependent upon techniques of performance evaluation, workload characterization,
and benchmarking. Many such studies implement queuing network-based simulation mod-
els of computer systems. However, stochastic analysis can be used instead of using simula-
tion models of computer systems. Using these models for various computing platforms, the
research study goals, probably resolved with an experimental design, could be:
1. to compare a number of systems and decide which system is best for a given set of
applications,
2. to determine for a specific system how well it is performing and whether any
improvements need to be made.
The Design choice influences which method of analysis are needed.
For each one of the SDLC phases, should the design approached be experimental or nonex-
perimental? If an independent variable can be manipulated, then an experimental approach
can and should be used. The variables in this study are numerous and complex, which indi-
cates to the study team that both experimental and nonexperimental designs are required.
Every adequate design must answer:
Does the design answer the research questions?
Will the design enable testing the hypotheses?
Researchers must remember to solve problems, not just apply techniques.

37082.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37082.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 629
37082.content:
The main objective of any study is to resolve the answer to the question not just apply tech-
niques. The method or technique is secondary.
Design research to answer the research questions.
Does the design adequately control independent variables?
Randomize whenever possible.
Control independent variables [which limits systematic variance from extraneous
and unwanted sources to have presence in the study].
Remember that a perfectly good design can and is often poorly used.
A good design must possess both internal validity and external validity.
If experimental design is required, then other potential questions are:
Should factors be included, if so what are the pertinent factors?
How many levels of each factor should be included?
How should the levels of the factors be spaced?
How should the experimental units be selected?
How many experimental units should be chosen for each treatment combination?
What steps should be taken to control experimental error?
What criterion measures should be used to evaluate the effects of the treatment
factors?
What if a modeling approach had been decided upon? Before undertaking more elaborate
testing, a good approach is to begin looking for obvious errors or oversights in the model.
When screening and evaluating candidate models, the researcher can:
Determine whether or not the current candidate model reveals any such mistakes as based
upon the problem statement.
Determine if all mathematical expressions are consistent with the units the model uses.
By varying the input parameters and/or the predictor variables, decide whether or not the
output from the model behaves in a acceptable manner.
Perform retrospective tests on the model to check if good results are produced.
Whatever methodology is used, researchers must address the validity issue. Internal validity
asks the question: Does the experimental manipulation really make a statistically significant
difference? If the study results and design are representative, or generalizable, then the
study possesses external validity.
To what populations can the results be generalized?
Are the variables of this research representative?

37083.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37083.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 631
37083.content:
chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 631
48.8 r eporting r esults
The team has planned, and then re-planned many times. Additionally the team has prepared.
At this point it would be time for DOING: implement the plan, perform the analysis, and
convey the results. The study will have: finished data validation, possibly created new vari-
ables, selected variables for the final model, removed outliers, chosen the “best” model or
models, and introduced knowing how to process categorical variables. Most of these tasks
required many decisions to be made for which no clear cut rules existed.
Decisions have an impact on research results and must be justified.
Research must be shared [discussed] with interested communities.
When reporting results, the study team must be sure the reader understands the results.
Tell them what you are going to tell them, tell them again, and then tell them what
you told them once more.
Present the most important results first, then present decreasingly important results. For
each set of results, remind the reader what research question the result is answering. After
all research questions have been presented, present any qualifications or elaborations using
a similar order.
Each finding should be presented first in prose, second in numbers, and then again in prose.
In the main results section of the teams final report, limited interpretation of results is per-
missible, it prepares the reader for the conclusion section.
Conclusions should logically follow from results.
The first paragraph of the discussion section must include a restatement of the research
question. A discussion should also include the teams efforts to relate the results to previous
research on the topic.
Keep the discussion section as brief as possible.
Toward the end of the discussion section the team should present what the team believed to
be some questions that remain unanswered despite the efforts made by the research study
team. It could be that questions are raised because of the results obtained by the study.
The discussion section should not contain any surprises for the reader.
Don’t allow detours.

48.9 p romoting r esearch r esults
This section contains the main points of the complete report but none of the qualifications
and elaborations necessary to fully understand those main points. This section is a teaser.
Hopefully the reader will use the executive summary to decide whether or not to read and/
or study the full report.
Make the executive summary informative and brief.
How? Rewrite, then rewrite, and finally you may have to rewrite again.
48.10 v ignette c losing
As a runner it surprises people when they inform others that being fit or to maintain good

37084.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37084.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 631
37084.content:
health are not why they are compulsive about running. Nor is it the acquisition of trophies and
competition that is important. Running is something they enjoy, something that they continu-
ously and perpetually practice on a consistent basis. Being a runner is part of one’s identity.
Suppose the study is completed. The reader has just witnessed and participated in extract-
ing knowledge from data. The reader should also have transferred the new knowledge to
other groups of individuals. Continue the journey by continuously performing a background
review, searching the Web, interacting with other researches in the study domain, and join-
ing a professional society and attending their conferences. Hopefully the reader will consider
not only enhancing their conceptual framework, but let research be part of their identity,
much as the runner claims identity with the “running lifestyle!”
48.11 c hapter s ummary
Research in the computing field evolved from ad hoc research to experimental research. ‘Ad
hoc’ research suffers from problems such as invalidity and irreproducibility. Use of experi-
mental designs, whenever possible, avoid these common pitfalls.
The breadth of the computing field includes: human factors research, operating systems,
computer systems organization, and data base management systems is only a short list. This
breadth of the field implies that researchers need to place an emphasis on measurement,
simulation, and analytical modeling as well as experimental research.
Additionally the reader has probably noticed the emphasis on project management in the
vignette. Technical projects are also business projects; they involve business issues such as
customer satisfaction, resource utilization, cost, profits, and many other business factors.
In the vignette the systems development cycle assumed as a framework for both the study
team and the project team. This framework can serve as a general scheme for illustrating
commonalities and differences among projects. Often individuals preparing for research are
either a technical person with little or no education in management or they are a person
primarily involved in product-development, marketing, process improvement, or related

37085.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
37085.heading: chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 633
37085.content:
chapter 48 n a r e S earch Stu D y V I gne t te n n n 633
projects, with limited background in technology. These individuals need to embark on a
study of project management.
Participants in research projects need to develop an appreciation for both the project man-
agement and the human and organizational side as well. Successful projects are those where
good communications, mutual trusts, and teamwork are present.
48.12 e xercises
Various types of research questions are represented in the following list.
a. For each question you are to determine if the actual computing environment, use of
simulation, or an analytic model should be used in the study.
b. Using this model describe how to resolve the research question based upon your
answer to Part A. The following list of activities may provide guidance in answering:
n design sets of experiments for measurement or simulation.
n check if the model is adequate.
n make comparative performance analyzes for the alternatives.
n control for measurement errors.
1. A performance evaluation for a personal workstation. To design this worksta-
tion answer: Which processor should be chosen? How much memory should
be recommended? How many external CD drives should be recommended?
Assume the workload can be of three types: secretarial, management, or
scientific. Also assume the end-user is either novice or expert. This is a system
design problem.
2. Determine the best database management system for a social work office infor-
mation referral system for seven counties for social services for senior citizens.
Consideration should be given to cost, availability, and compatibility. (Hint:
Look into required workloads and benchmarks). This is a system selection
problem.
3. Find for your organization about the current computing system. Consider a
system upgrade study. Either replacing the whole system or parts of the current
system with newer but compatible units. Assume the compatibility consider-
ations are dictated by the vendor. You are to recommend quantity, speed, and
other pertinent attribute values.
4. For the DBMS application in problem (2) using the required workload using
appropriate attributes and the social work office resource management policies,
optimize the performance of the query and data manipulation processing. This
is a system tuning problem.

5. Your office workstation is unacceptably sluggish. Develop a method to deter-
mine whether inadequate resources of poor system management is the reason.
You can monitor the system and examine the behavior of various resource man-
agement policies under different loading conditions. This is a system analysis
problem.
6. Your company is considering the expansion of an existing computing facility.

problem. Consider the case where direct measurements are possible and when
